questions.question: In an equilibrium, what is a role of a catalyst?
questions.answer: **D.** A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position is unchanged.
options: It slows the rate of reaction.
It ensures the reaction is exothermic.
It moves the equilibrium of a reaction in the forward direction.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

questions.question:
In an acid–base titration the acid was in a burette and a pipette was used to deliver a known quantity of base into a conical flask. Which gives the final rinse liquid for each piece of equipment?

(Each option lists burette / pipette / conical flask.)
questions.answer: **B.** Rinse the burette and pipette with the solutions they will deliver, and the flask with water.

questions.question: Which of the following is a biofuel?
questions.answer: **B.** A biofuel is a fuel made from recently living biomass such as cellulose.

questions.question: In which reaction does the equilibrium lie furthest to the left?
questions.answer: **B.** The smallest $K_{eq}$ indicates the equilibrium that most favours reactants.

questions.question:
Consider the gaseous reaction $\text{A}_2+3\text{B}\rightleftharpoons\text{A}_2\text{B}_3$. Quantities of all three chemicals are placed in a 1.0 L vessel at 1000 K and the system is allowed to come to equilibrium. The graph shows the concentrations with time.

Which expression gives the equilibrium constant at 1000 K?
questions.answer: **C.** $K=\dfrac{[\text{A}_2\text{B}_3]}{[\text{A}_2][\text{B}]^3}$ using the equilibrium values 0.5, 0.1 and 0.2.

questions.question: PES (a polyester) is a condensation polymer. Part of its structure is shown, followed by a table of possible monomer pairs. What are the two monomers of this polymer?
questions.answer: **D.** The chain alternates a four-carbon diacid unit and a two-carbon diol unit: butanedioic acid and ethane-1,2-diol.

questions.question: Which is an example of an amphiprotic species?
questions.answer: **A.** $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ can donate a proton (to give $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$) or accept one (to give $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$).

questions.question:
Consider these equilibrium systems.

| Equation | Reaction | $\Delta H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$ | $-180$ |
| 2 | $\text{CO}(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)+\text{H}_2(g)$ | $-46$ |
| 3 | $\text{PCl}_5(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$ | $+93$ |
| 4 | $\text{CH}_4(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$ | $-891$ |

After equilibrium was established, the temperature was decreased and the pressure increased. In which system would both changes increase the yield?
questions.answer: **A.** It is exothermic (cooling favours products) and has fewer moles of gas on the product side (higher pressure favours products).

questions.question: Lead could be separated from a mixture of $\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2(aq)$, $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2(aq)$, $\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(aq)$ and $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq)$ by precipitating with a room-temperature solution of:
questions.answer: **B.** Of these cations only $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ forms an insoluble chloride. Sulfate, carbonate and phosphate would also precipitate other cations.

questions.question: The molar solubility of $\text{PbF}_2$ is $2.1\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. What is its $K_{sp}$?
Which of these acids has the weakest conjugate base?
questions.answer: **A.** The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base; HCl is a strong acid.

questions.question: 10 mL of a 0.05 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of sulfuric acid was made up to 1000 mL with distilled water. What was the pH of the resulting solution?
questions.answer: **B.** $[\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4]=5\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Taking both protons as fully ionised, $[\text{H}^+]=1\times10^{-3}$ and pH $=3.0$.

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide is formed when nitrogen monoxide is oxidised:
$$2\text{NO}(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)\qquad\Delta H=-62\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A change was imposed on an equilibrium mixture of NO, O$_2$ and NO$_2$. The mixture returned to equilibrium and another change was imposed. The graph shows the effects of the two changes.

What do the initial concentrations of the three gases indicate?
questions.answer: **C.** All concentrations are constant before the first change, so the system is at equilibrium.
options: That the $\text{NO}_2$ gas reaches equilibrium first.
That there is initially no NO gas present in the system.
The relative proportions of the three gases at equilibrium.
That $\text{O}_2$ and NO are producing $\text{NO}_2$ faster than they are being formed.

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide is formed when nitrogen monoxide is oxidised:
$$2\text{NO}(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)\qquad\Delta H=-62\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A change was imposed on an equilibrium mixture of NO, O$_2$ and NO$_2$. The mixture returned to equilibrium and another change was imposed. The graph shows the effects of the two changes.

Which changes best account for the shape of the graph? (Each option lists the first change; the second change.)
questions.answer:
**D.** At the first change $\text{NO}_2$ falls while NO and $\text{O}_2$ rise gradually: the exothermic equilibrium shifts left, so the temperature was raised. At the second change [NO] drops suddenly, and the system shifts left to replace some of it.

*Note: the graph is drawn with NO finishing above its level just before it was removed. Removing NO alone can only partly restore it, so the final level should be lower.*
options: The temperature is decreased; $[\text{O}_2]$ is increased.
The temperature is decreased; [NO] is decreased.
The temperature is increased; $[\text{O}_2]$ is increased.
The temperature is increased; [NO] is decreased.

questions.question: What volume of oxygen gas (at 25 °C and 100 kPa) is required for the complete combustion of 16.0 g of methanol?
questions.answer: **C.** $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}+\tfrac32\text{O}_2\rightarrow\text{CO}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $n(\text{O}_2)=1.5\times\dfrac{16.0}{32.04}=0.749$ mol, so $V=0.749\times24.79\approx18.6$ L.

questions.question: Which solution is basic at 25 °C?
In which pair of molecules does the dotted line correctly show a hydrogen bond?
questions.answer: **C.** A hydrogen bond links an H bonded to N, O or F with a lone pair on N, O or F: here an N–H hydrogen to the alcohol oxygen.

questions.question: A student performed a titration using computer-based technology and obtained the graph shown (pH against volume added). What can be deduced from the graph?
questions.answer: **A.** The initial pH of about 3 with a buffer region, and an equivalence point above 7, indicate a weak acid titrated with a strong base.
options: The acid was a weak acid and the end point was at pH 9.
The acid was a strong acid and the end point was at pH 9.
The acid was a weak acid and the end point was at pH 2.5.
The acid was a strong acid and the end point was at pH 11.

questions.question: An organic compound has the molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$. What is a possible name for it?
questions.answer: **D.** Propyl methanoate, $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$.

questions.question: How many structural isomers have the formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_9\text{N}$?
questions.answer: **C.** Propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine, N-methylethanamine and N,N-dimethylmethanamine.

questions.question: Using a named example, explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have used solubility equilibria.
questions.answer:
**Cycad seeds** are a food source but contain a water-soluble toxin (cycasin). Aboriginal Peoples crushed or cut the seeds and left them in running water for several days.

The toxin dissolves from the seed into the water. Because the flowing water continually carries the dissolved toxin away, equilibrium between toxin in the seed and in solution is never established, so dissolution keeps going until the food is safe to eat.

questions.question: An organic compound contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and each molecule contains two oxygen atoms. Its mass spectrum is shown. Identify the compound and justify your choice.
questions.answer:
The compound is **ethanoic acid**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.

- The molecular ion is at $m/z=60$. Two O atoms account for 32, leaving 28 ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$), so the formula is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$.
- The peak at 45 is $\text{COOH}^+$ (loss of $\text{CH}_3$, 15), the peak at 43 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ (loss of OH, 17) and the peak at 15 is $\text{CH}_3^+$.
- The isomer methyl methanoate would be expected to give a strong peak at 31 ($\text{CH}_3\text{O}^+$), which is only very weak here.

questions.question: When magnesium chloride dissolves in water, changes occur in both the bonding and the entropy. Explain these changes, supporting your answer with a labelled diagram.
questions.answer:
**Bonding.** In solid $\text{MgCl}_2$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are held in a lattice by ionic bonds, and water molecules are hydrogen bonded to one another. On dissolving, the ionic bonds and some hydrogen bonds are broken and new **ion–dipole attractions** form: the $\delta-$ oxygen of water surrounds each $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and the $\delta+$ hydrogens surround each $\text{Cl}^-$. The energy released by hydration exceeds that needed to separate the ions, so dissolution is exothermic.

**Entropy.** Two effects oppose each other. The ions leave an ordered lattice and spread through the solution (entropy increases). Water molecules become held in ordered shells around the ions (entropy decreases), especially around the small, highly charged $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. For $\text{MgCl}_2$ the ordering of water is larger, so the entropy of the system **decreases** overall. The process is still spontaneous because it is strongly exothermic, which raises the entropy of the surroundings by more.

*Note: the school's answer says entropy increases. Standard data give a negative $\Delta S$ for dissolving $\text{MgCl}_2$ (about $-115$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$).*

questions.question: Which of lead(II) sulfate and lead(II) chloride is more soluble in water at 25 °C? Give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer:
**Lead(II) chloride.** From $K_{sp}$:

- $\text{PbCl}_2$: $4s^3=1.70\times10^{-5}\Rightarrow s=1.62\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $\text{PbSO}_4$: $s^2=2.53\times10^{-8}\Rightarrow s=1.59\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$

*Note: the school compares the $K_{sp}$ values directly. That is not valid in general for salts with different ion ratios, so molar solubilities should be compared.*

questions.question: Quantitatively compare the molar solubility of lead(II) sulfate in water with its solubility in a 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of sodium sulfate at 25 °C.
questions.answer:
**In water:** $K_{sp}=s^2=2.53\times10^{-8}$, so $s=1.59\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

**In 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$:**

| | $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]$ | $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$ |
|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0 | 0.10 |
| Change | $+s$ | $+s$ |
| Equilibrium | $s$ | $0.10+s\approx0.10$ |

$s=\dfrac{2.53\times10^{-8}}{0.10}=2.53\times10^{-7}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$\text{PbSO}_4$ is about 630 times less soluble in the sodium sulfate solution, because of the common ion effect.

questions.question:
Sulfur trioxide is made from sulfur dioxide and oxygen with a catalyst:
$$2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)\qquad\Delta H=-196\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A mixture of 2.00 mol of $\text{SO}_2$ and 2.00 mol of $\text{O}_2$ was placed in a 4.00 L vessel and kept at 1000 K until equilibrium was reached. The vessel then contained 1.66 mol of $\text{SO}_3$.

Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at 1000 K.

Sulfur trioxide is made from sulfur dioxide and oxygen with a catalyst:
$$2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)\qquad\Delta H=-196\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A mixture of 2.00 mol of $\text{SO}_2$ and 2.00 mol of $\text{O}_2$ was placed in a 4.00 L vessel and kept at 1000 K until equilibrium was reached. The vessel then contained 1.66 mol of $\text{SO}_3$.

A manufacturer changes these conditions to increase the percentage yield in a closed system whose volume may be changed. What changes would increase the yield of $\text{SO}_3$? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
**Lower the temperature.** The forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle cooling shifts the equilibrium right to release heat, and $K_{eq}$ increases. A compromise temperature is needed because the rate falls (fewer successful collisions).

**Decrease the volume (increase the pressure).** There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the equilibrium shifts right to reduce the number of gas particles. $K_{eq}$ is unchanged.

(Adding excess $\text{O}_2$ would also raise the percentage conversion of $\text{SO}_2$.)

questions.question:
A molecule of citric acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$, is shown. Its first dissociation in water is
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

Identify a conjugate acid–base pair in this equation, naming which species is the acid and which the conjugate base.
questions.answer: Acid $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$ with conjugate base $\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-$ (or acid $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ with conjugate base $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

questions.question:
A molecule of citric acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$, is shown. Its first dissociation in water is
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

$K_a=5.01\times10^{-4}$ for the first dissociation at 298 K. Explain the strength of citric acid, including the $K_a$ expression in your answer.
questions.answer:
$$K_a=\frac{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7]}=5.01\times10^{-4}$$

Citric acid is a **weak** acid. $K_a$ is much less than 1, so the equilibrium lies well to the left: only a small fraction of the molecules ionise, and most remain as un-ionised $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$, giving a relatively low $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ for its concentration.

questions.question:
A molecule of citric acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$, is shown. Its first dissociation in water is
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

Citric acid and its conjugate base can be used as a buffer. Justify this statement.
questions.answer:
A buffer is a solution containing significant, comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

Citric acid is weak, so a mixture of citric acid and a citrate salt (such as sodium dihydrogen citrate) holds large reserves of both $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-$ at equilibrium.

**Added acid:** the extra $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ reacts with the conjugate base, shifting the equilibrium left:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Added base:** the $\text{OH}^-$ is neutralised by the weak acid:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{O}_7^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
(equivalently, $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and the equilibrium shifts right to replace it).

In both cases $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ changes very little, so the statement is justified, provided the amounts added are small compared with the amounts of acid and conjugate base.

questions.question:
A student determined the concentration of an unknown sulfuric acid solution as follows.

1. She weighed out 4.00 g of sodium carbonate.
2. She dissolved it in a little distilled water and made it up to 1000 mL in a volumetric flask. This became her 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ standard solution.
3. She titrated 25.0 mL of this solution with the unknown sulfuric acid, using bromothymol blue as indicator.

| Titration | Volume of sulfuric acid used (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 5.6 |
| 2 | 5.2 |
| 3 | 4.8 |

Assess the validity and reliability of this method and results.
questions.answer:
**Validity of the method: not valid.**

- 4.00 g of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ in 1.00 L is $\dfrac{4.00}{105.99}=0.038$ mol L$^{-1}$, not 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$, so any concentration calculated from 0.10 is badly wrong.
- Bromothymol blue changes at pH 6–7.6. A strong acid titrating the weak base carbonate has its equivalence point (to $\text{CO}_2$/water) at about pH 4, so methyl orange should be used.
- The sodium carbonate should be dried before weighing to act as a primary standard.

**Reliability of the results: not reliable.** The titres differ by up to 0.8 mL and keep falling, so none are concordant (within about 0.1 mL). The method gives no rough titration and no further repeats until concordance. The very small titres (about 5 mL) also make the percentage uncertainty large; the acid should be diluted to give titres near 20–25 mL.

*Note: the school suggests phenolphthalein. Its range (pH 8.3–10) is on the basic side and is unsuitable for a strong acid–weak base titration to the second equivalence point; methyl orange is appropriate.*

questions.question:
A conductivity graph can be used to determine sodium ion concentration in water samples. A sample of bore water was collected and 10 mL of it was diluted with deionised water to 1000 mL in a volumetric flask. Standard sodium ion solutions were also prepared.

| $\text{Na}^+$ concentration (ppm) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conductivity | 0 | 0.26 | 0.48 | 0.71 | 0.95 | 1.2 |

The diluted bore sample had a conductivity of 0.78. Guidelines (based on taste) for sodium in drinking water are:

- less than $2.6\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$: good
- $2.6\times10^{-2}$ to $3.9\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$: fair
- $3.9\times10^{-2}$ to $5.2\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$: poor
- greater than $5.2\times10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$: unacceptable

By graphing the data and performing relevant calculations, assess the suitability of the original bore water for drinking.
questions.answer:
Plot conductivity against concentration and draw the line of best fit (graph below). A conductivity of 0.78 corresponds to about **6.5 ppm** in the diluted sample.

Dilution factor $=\dfrac{1000}{10}=100$, so the original water has $6.5\times100=650$ ppm $=0.65$ g L$^{-1}$.
$$[\text{Na}^+]=\frac{0.65}{22.99}=2.8\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

This lies in the **fair** range: the bore water is acceptable for drinking, though not of good quality in taste, and it is close to the good/fair boundary.

This assumes that conductivity is due only to sodium ions. Other dissolved ions in bore water would also conduct, so the result is likely to overestimate $[\text{Na}^+]$, and the guideline says nothing about other contaminants.

questions.question:
A white powder contained mostly magnesium oxide mixed with an impurity that does not react with acid. 2.65 g of the powder was reacted with 50 mL of 2.0 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid, and the mixture was diluted to 250 mL in a volumetric flask. 25 mL samples were titrated against 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein.

| Titration | Volume of NaOH (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 17.2 |
| 2 | 15.5 |
| 3 | 15.4 |

Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium oxide in the powder.
questions.answer:
$\text{MgO}+2\text{HCl}\rightarrow\text{MgCl}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}$

Initial $n(\text{HCl})=0.050\times2.0=0.100$ mol.

Average concordant titre (discard 17.2): $\dfrac{15.5+15.4}{2}=15.45$ mL.

$n(\text{NaOH})=0.01545\times0.10=1.545\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{HCl})$ in 25 mL.

Excess HCl in 250 mL $=1.545\times10^{-2}$ mol.

HCl reacted with MgO $=0.100-0.01545=0.08455$ mol.

$n(\text{MgO})=0.04228$ mol, $m=0.04228\times40.31=1.70$ g.
$$\%\ \text{MgO}=\frac{1.70}{2.65}\times100\approx64\%$$

questions.question: Water can be added to but-1-ene to form two products. Give the structural formulae of the major and minor products and identify a relevant catalyst.
questions.answer:
- **Major product:** butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$
- **Minor product:** butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
- **Catalyst:** dilute sulfuric acid.

questions.question:
The solubility of some alcohols in water at 25 °C is shown.

| Formula | Name | Solubility (g/100 mL) |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ | methanol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ | ethanol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{OH}$ | propan-1-ol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{OH}$ | butan-1-ol | 7.3 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{OH}$ | pentan-1-ol | 2.2 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{OH}$ | hexan-1-ol | 0.59 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{OH}$ | heptan-1-ol | 0.17 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{OH}$ | octan-1-ol | 0.03 |

Describe one procedure to ensure safe handling of these substances.
questions.answer:
Keep the alcohols away from naked flames and heat them only with a water bath or heating mantle, because they are volatile and flammable and their vapour can ignite.

(Working in a fume cupboard to avoid inhaling vapours is also acceptable.)

questions.question:
The solubility of some alcohols in water at 25 °C is shown.

| Formula | Name | Solubility (g/100 mL) |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ | methanol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ | ethanol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{OH}$ | propan-1-ol | greater than 10 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{OH}$ | butan-1-ol | 7.3 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{OH}$ | pentan-1-ol | 2.2 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{OH}$ | hexan-1-ol | 0.59 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{OH}$ | heptan-1-ol | 0.17 |
| $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{OH}$ | octan-1-ol | 0.03 |

Explain the trend in solubility in terms of intermolecular forces.
questions.answer:
Solubility decreases as the carbon chain lengthens.

The polar –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water, which favours dissolving. The non-polar hydrocarbon chain interacts with water only through weak forces and disrupts the hydrogen bonding between water molecules, while chains attract one another by dispersion forces.

As the chain gets longer, the non-polar part and its dispersion forces dominate more over the single –OH group, so less alcohol dissolves.

questions.question: 1-bromobutane reacts with dilute sodium hydroxide. Name the products of this reaction.
questions.answer: **Butan-1-ol** and **sodium bromide**.

questions.question: The structural formulae of two organic compounds, A and B, are shown. Justify a test that could be used to distinguish between them, giving the result. Include an equation.
questions.answer:
A contains a **secondary** alcohol group and B a **tertiary** alcohol group. Both have a –COOH group, so tests for carboxylic acids would not distinguish them.

**Test:** warm each with acidified potassium dichromate.

- A: the orange solution turns **green**, because a secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone.
- B: **no change** (stays orange), because the carbon carrying the OH has no hydrogen, so a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised.

$$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(OH)COOH}\xrightarrow{\ [\text{O}],\ \text{H}^+\ }(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOCOOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

*Note: the school describes acidified dichromate as yellow; it is orange.*

**Equation**
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}+\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\overset{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ \text{heat}}{\rightleftharpoons}\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Procedure:** place butanoic acid, excess ethanol, a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid and boiling chips in a round-bottomed flask. Heat under reflux for about 30 minutes, then pour into water or sodium carbonate solution in a separating funnel, separate the ester layer, dry it and distil.

**Justification of conditions and equipment**

- Heating increases the rate of this slow reaction.
- The reflux condenser (open at the top) condenses volatile reactants and ester and returns them, so nothing is lost and pressure does not build up.
- Concentrated sulfuric acid is a catalyst and also absorbs water, shifting the equilibrium towards the ester. Excess ethanol does the same.
- Boiling chips give smooth boiling; sodium carbonate removes unreacted acid.

**Risk assessment**

| Hazard | Control |
|---|---|
| Ethanol and ester are flammable | heating mantle or water bath, no naked flames |
| Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is corrosive | gloves, safety glasses, add drop by drop |
| Butanoic acid is corrosive and foul smelling | use a fume cupboard |
| Pressure build-up | never stopper the condenser |

questions.question:
Ethene, from fossil hydrocarbon sources, is converted to vinyl chloride, the starting material for polyvinyl chloride (PVC):
$$\text{Cl}_2(g)+\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(g)\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{Cl}(g)+\text{HCl}(g)$$

What is the IUPAC systematic name for vinyl chloride?
questions.answer: **Chloroethene**

questions.question:
Ethene, from fossil hydrocarbon sources, is converted to vinyl chloride, the starting material for polyvinyl chloride (PVC):
$$\text{Cl}_2(g)+\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(g)\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{Cl}(g)+\text{HCl}(g)$$

How could you test that all the ethene had been converted to vinyl chloride?
questions.answer:
Analyse the purified gas by **gas chromatography** (or GC–mass spectrometry), comparing with pure samples. Complete conversion is shown by a peak at the retention time of chloroethene and **no peak** at the retention time of ethene (and no molecular ion at $m/z=28$ from a separate ethene component).

(${}^{13}$C NMR would also work: ethene gives one signal, chloroethene two, so no extra ethene signal should remain.)

*Note: the school suggests bromine water. This cannot work, because chloroethene also contains a C=C bond and would decolourise bromine water too.*

questions.question:
Ethene, from fossil hydrocarbon sources, is converted to vinyl chloride, the starting material for polyvinyl chloride (PVC):
$$\text{Cl}_2(g)+\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(g)\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{Cl}(g)+\text{HCl}(g)$$

Vinyl chloride is then polymerised to PVC as shown, with $n=1200$. What volume of ethene, measured at 25 °C and 100 kPa, is required to make 1.00 kg of PVC with an average molar mass of 75.00 kg mol$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{PVC})=\dfrac{1.00}{75.00}=0.01333$ mol

$n(\text{chloroethene})=1200\times0.01333=16.0$ mol $=n(\text{ethene})$

$V=16.0\times24.79=397$ L

questions.question:
An experiment was conducted to find the heat of neutralisation. A solution was made by dissolving 3.79 g of barium hydroxide in 100 mL of water. 30.0 mL of this solution was reacted with 27.0 mL of 0.400 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid. The heat of neutralisation was calculated to be 51.7 kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Calculate the temperature change and the pH of the resulting solution.
questions.answer:
$\text{Ba(OH)}_2+2\text{HNO}_3\rightarrow\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2)$ in 30.0 mL $=\dfrac{3.79}{171.35}\times\dfrac{30.0}{100}=6.64\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.01327$ mol.

$n(\text{HNO}_3)=0.0270\times0.400=0.0108$ mol: the acid is limiting, so $n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=0.0108$ mol.

$q=0.0108\times51.7\times10^3=558$ J. Taking 57.0 mL of solution as 57.0 g with $c=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$:
$$\Delta T=\frac{558}{57.0\times4.18}=2.34\ ^\circ\text{C rise}$$

Excess $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.01327-0.0108=2.47\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $[\text{OH}^-]=\dfrac{2.47\times10^{-3}}{0.0570}=0.0434$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$\text{pOH}=1.36$, so $\text{pH}=12.64$.
